title: US Consul-General Auckland ↔ Naval Commander San Francisco / Washington, cipher cables on unknown wireless signals heard in New Zealand; the reply could not be read by its recipient
correspondents: Alfred A. Winslow, American Consul-General, Auckland → Naval Commander, San Francisco (18 Feb 1918); unidentified US Government office, Washington D.C. (probably the Navy Department) → American Consul-General, Auckland (received 1 Mar 1918)
shelfmark: NARA, RG 59, Central Decimal File 1910-29, 763.72 (European War), microfilm M367 roll 83, file unit '763.72/9366-9450: Feb.-Apr. 1918' (naId 27107744); Auckland despatches No. 370 (26 Feb 1918) and No. 375 (4 Mar 1918) with enclosures
folio_note: M367 roll 83 f.0110 (No. 370, 'Mysterious Wireless Calls in South Pacific', 26 Feb 1918); f.0111 (enclosure: Staff Paymaster W. J. Brown for the Naval Adviser to the NZ Government, HMS Philomel, Wellington, 14 Feb 1918, asking whether an unknown automatic W/T transmission heard on 2000 m on 11/12 Feb was US Californian-Honolulu traffic); f.0112 (No. 375, 4 Mar 1918, 'Coded Cablegram with reference to Wireless Stations'); f.0113 (copy of the cable sent 18 Feb 1918 to the Naval Commander, San Francisco: c. 20 five-letter groups, 98 letters, 'FVFRO TFKFX JTQII ...'); f.0114 (copy of the reply received 1 Mar 1918 from Washington 'usgovt', 37 counted words: ten-letter groups 'Ssblnodyym dncrvjjwij nakgtrtlme ...', c. 360 letters).
status: Found in the slice L caps/word rerun of RG 59 (the early groups' missing detectors). Whole reel OCR read (fetched 27 Oct 2026). Winslow writes on 4 Mar that the reply is one 'which I am at a loss to know from whence it came, further than it was sent from Washington, D.C., I rather suppose from the Navy Department', and asks that it be passed to them: the recipient could not decipher it, and no clear text or decode is filed on the reel. The outgoing cable's content is known in substance from the Philomel letter (a crib: wireless, 2000 metres, Honolulu, automatic working). known.py: no hits for 763.72/9366, 27107744, Winslow; not in catalogue.json or earlier nara_* triage.
why: A US Government cipher cable of 1918 that its own addressee could not read, filed with its context: a small test of US Navy/State cipher systems of the First World War, with a near-crib for the outgoing message.
prior_art: open (checked 27 Oct 2026: known.py, catalogue.json, nara_* sweep folders)

title: Coahuila state code telegrams on the Mexican Kickapoo affair, Múzquiz ↔ Saltillo, 1906: two-digit code passages that the Mexican Embassy could not decipher
correspondents: L. A. Guajardo (Jefe Político, Múzquiz) and Judge F. Valdés Llano → Governor Miguel Cárdenas, Saltillo; Cárdenas → Guajardo; R. C. Conine → Guajardo; Guajardo → Ignacio E. Rivas
date: 25 Jun - 27 Jul 1906 (copies sent to the State Department 8 Nov 1907)
shelfmark: NARA, RG 59, Numerical File 1906-1910, case 3706/35-45 (Kickapoo Indians), microfilm M862 roll 342; file unit naId 19505183
folio_note: M862 roll 342 f.0500-0504 (Teller's letter of 8 Nov 1907 from Douglas, Arizona, enclosing the telegrams for deciphering, and the Department's memoranda); f.0505-0513 (copies of the telegrams numbered 35-45: 25 June, 30 June (2), 2 July, 11 July, 17 July, 19 July and Sabinas 27 July 1906; code passages as runs of two-digit numbers inside clear Spanish/English text, e.g. 'Conviene 70 48 35 40 34 30 98 99 70 90 73 49 ...'; c. 270 groups in the OCR, perhaps 400-450 on the frames); f.0514-0517 (Root's telegram and letter to Teller, 14 Nov 1907: 'The Mexican Embassy here does not know the code and is unable to decipher it').
status: Found in the slice L word-hit triage of RG 59 (research/nara_triage_l/agent_59.md); the reel OCR was read again here (27 Oct 2026). The Senate subcommittee on the Mexican Kickapoo land frauds (Teller) obtained copies from the Federal telegraph office at Múzquiz and asked the Department for a decipherment; the Mexican Embassy could not read the code, suggested a state governors' code, and the copies were returned to Teller. Nothing later on the roll deciphers them. Repeated numbers inside words (10 35 30 18 / 10 35 70 18) and code mixed into clear text suggest a simple two-digit letter or syllable substitution with Spanish plaintext. known.py: no hits for Kickapoo, Múzquiz, Guajardo; not in catalogue.json.
why: A Mexican state governor's telegraph code of 1906, unread by the Mexican Embassy and the State Department, filed with the clear context of a US Senate investigation into Kickapoo land frauds; likely readable from the ciphertext alone.
language: Spanish (clear passages translated into English for the Senate)
prior_art: open (checked 27 Oct 2026: known.py, catalogue.json, nara_* sweep folders, one web search on the Kickapoo hearings; the printed hearings not yet checked)

title: Hieronimo Ranzo (?) to 'Garbino', intercepted imperial letter
correspondents: Hieronimo Ranzo (probably; Gattinara's man) → 'Garbino'
shelfmark: BnF fr. 3022 no. 20 (ff. 44r–46v; addition sheet and jargon ff. 48–50v)
status: The other two items first catalogued here (nos. 6 and 10, del Vasto to Charles V) are read: no. 10 by Lasry (2023) with Tomokiyo's edited text, no. 6 in targets/vasto1527/ (its own page since 14 Oct 2026). No. 20 is an Italian letter, Madrid 11 Apr 1528, to 'Garbino', in the same code as Hieronimo Ranzo's letters (fr. 2988). The code is initial letter + number with non-alphabetical numbering; ~3,900 groups are transcribed. The key was recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry and, independently, by Paolo Rosson (6 Oct 2026; PRs #35, #45), and no. 20 measures 94.4% (targets/ranzo1528/, 18 Oct 2026), just under the read bar. No French decipherment exists; Clair. 327 ff. 279-280 is an undeciphered copy.
why: Five months after the Sack of Rome, during Lautrec's campaign in Italy.
known: No. 6 (del Vasto, Cipher 2) deciphered here with Lasry's key, 98.0% (vasto1527.html); no. 10 (Cipher 1) key recovered by Lasry 2023, read in part with Tomokiyo's text. No. 20: Ranzo's code key recovered from ciphertext only by George Lasry and, independently, Paolo Rosson (6 Oct 2026); no. 20 measured here at 94.4% (ranzo1528.html, PRs #35, #45).
open: No. 20 (Garbino letter): 74 of 1,314 tokens, 27 groups with no value in either key and 47 tentative Lasry values Rosson's key does not confirm; both keys' readings still to be checked against the images of ff. 44r-46v. Blocker: open codes.

title: Espagnol 318 nos. 92, 93, 94: Ferdinand's secretariat ciphers (Great Captain 1500, Suárez de Figueroa 1504, viceroy of Sicily 1503)
correspondents: Lorenzo Suárez de Figueroa (Venice) → the Catholic Monarchs
shelfmark: BnF Espagnol 318 no. 93
status: Widened again 23 Oct 2026 (Reading audit 22-23 Oct 2026 (George Lasry's test: a reading must build sentences): no. 92 and no. 94 are decoded, not read, so they are back here). Narrowed 21 Oct 2026 to no. 93. The entry first covered five ciphered letters in at least four ciphers: no. 5 (Escrivà's cipher, printed by Parisi 2020; targets/federico1497/), no. 92 (Cifra general, read in part; targets/esp318/) and no. 95 (recto deciphered in full by George Lasry with his CTTS key, PR #75, 22 Oct 2026; verso by Michael Brackx; targets/esp318no95/) have their own entries, and no. 94 (the viceroy of Sicily, Messina 1503) was split off on 21 Oct 2026 after Michael Brackx recovered its key ciphertext-only and read part of its code (issue #62; targets/esp318no94/). No. 93 is unread and its key unknown: code initials exclude Escrivà no. 1 and the Cifra general; a homophonic anneal of 1,016 signs failed (the CVC groups are atomic); no. 94's key does not fit and the two code inventories barely overlap. See targets/esp318no93/.
why: The earliest Spanish diplomatic ciphers online; the Naples war (Cerignola, Garigliano) and Venice 1504.
known: Nothing for nos. 93 and 94: keys not identified; a homophonic anneal of 1,016 signs of no. 93 failed (esp318no93.html). Former siblings: no. 5 printed by Parisi 2020 (federico1497), no. 92 about 75% deciphered with the Cifra general (esp318), no. 95 recto deciphered in full by George Lasry with his own key (esp318no95, PR #75).
open: No. 93 (f. 118r-v) whole letter: CVC nomenclator, the suspected Gran cifra key survives only as Bergenroth's partial list (BNE MSS 20.211/52, not online). No. 92 (targets/esp318/): decoded with the Cifra general (Galende Díaz 1994), not yet built into sentences. No. 94 (targets/esp318no94/): Michael Brackx's key recovered ciphertext-only, about 90 code groups open; his decryption has holes in most sentences.
